newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - SBC aims for Japan market with LTCB.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - SBC aims for Japan market with LTCB.

text.p: Globally active Swiss Bank Corporation (SBC) on Tuesday unveiled a joint venture with Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan (LTCB) in a bid to become a major player in Tokyo after Japan's "Big Bang" financial deregulation.

"We are very serious about becoming a major domestic presence in Japan because we are really convinced that this Big Bang is for real," said Luqman Arnold, Asia/Pacific chairman of SBC's investment banking division SBC Warburg.
"Building (SBC's own business) is not a realistic option if one wants to be a major player during and after the Big Bang," Arnold told financial analysts in a telephone conference.

The Big Bang is Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's programme to make Japanese markets "free, fair and global" by breaking down walls among banks, brokers and insurers and introducing more competition.
SBC and LTCB signed a letter of intent to swap three-percent equity stakes and set up three joint ventures based in Japan to serve Japanese corporate, institutional and wealthier private customers.

Analysts of the European bank sector said the deal was the most extensive alliance sealed yet by Western banks as Japanese regulatory barriers gradually melt under reforms which were launched this year and could be completed by 2000.
"Conceptually it is an interesting approach. I think it will be a while before we see how it actually works," said John Leonard at Salomon Bros in London.
In a Tokyo statement, LTCB and SBC said the three joint ventures would cover Japan-based business in investment banking, asset management and private banking -- SBC's three global business areas.
SBC also has a large retail business in Switzerland, where it is one of the country's three biggest banks.
SBC said its total assets of $266 billion compared with $252 billion at LTCB, a wholesale domestic bank with a large base of corporate and institutional customers.
"We would never have been able to build this client base on our own," SBC Warburg's Arnold told analysts.
Under the pact, the partners will set up a jointly managed investment bank, LTCB SBC Warburg Securities, in early 1998.

With capital of 60 billion yen, the venture will be responsible for the Japanese investment banking of both companies worldwide, combining LTCB Securities Co with SBC's existing Japanese equity, interest rate, foreign exchange, derivatives and corporate finance operations.
LTCB and SBC will also set up an asset management firm, LTCB SBC Brinson, and Japan's first-ever private bank after a market survey to determine customer needs more precisely.
The financial side foresees LTCB raising about 200 billion yen in capital, or $1.8 billion, subject to board approval.
Of this, 130 billion yen would be raised through preferred stock and 70 billion yen through subordinated debt.
SBC Warburg will help LTCB raise the funds and SBC will hold about 50 percent of the new LTCB preferred stock in its investment portfolio, the statement said.
"We are not paying a premium for LCTB and we are not paying goodwill," Arnold told the analysts.
LTCB's three percent stake in SBC shares may come from SBC's own holdings or from already-approved capital.
SBC chief financial officer Peter Wufli told the same presentation SBC still had two million shares in approved capital with a nominal value of 100 million Swiss francs.
